one_liner: Header-only C++11 framework for crash-recoverable point-to-point messaging over TCP or shared memory; claims ~4.8x lower RTT than ZeroMQ.
what_it_does: A Linux client/server framework for a persistent, named connection between two processes: you derive from the TcpShmClient or TcpShmServer template (CRTP), supply a compile-time Conf struct, and implement callbacks such as OnClientMsg and OnSeqNumberMismatch. Every sent message stays in a memory-mapped send queue until the peer acks it by sequence number, so after a disconnect or a process crash the session resumes and unacked messages are resent without user code. Same-host peers can pick SHM mode, which moves the data path onto a pair of shared-memory queues and keeps TCP only for login and heartbeats, behind the same Alloc()/Push() and Front()/Pop() zero-copy API. It is not a drop-in for ZeroMQ: there are no socket patterns (PUB/SUB, REQ/REP), no routing or fan-out, and messages are raw binary blobs tagged with a user msg_type.
how_it_is_fast: SHM mode uses a bounded single-producer/single-consumer variable-length ring buffer (SPSCVarQueue, from the author's SPSC_Queue project) in a shm_open segment: 64-byte cache-line blocks, read and write indices on separate 128-byte-aligned lines, a producer-side cached read index, and messages built in place, synchronized only by compiler barriers with no atomics, locks or syscalls on the data path. Both sides busy-poll, so there is no kernel wakeup cost. TCP mode is a non-blocking, TCP_NODELAY socket polled from the user's thread, with the ack sequence piggybacked in each 8-byte message header, optional batching via PushMore(), and a send queue that is an mmap-ed file with no fsync/msync. The library creates no threads and does no logging, exceptions or clock reads.
when_to_use: Same-host IPC between two C++ processes where latency dominates, for example a trading gateway and a strategy, and you can give a core to each busy-polling thread. SHM mode measured 0.34 us average RTT on the author's machine.

Point-to-point streams or request/response of small binary structs (under 64 KB including the 8-byte header) that must resume automatically after either side crashes or reconnects, without running a broker.
Sessions that should reset on a schedule: renaming the server (for example 'Server20180714') discards the previous session's unhandled messages, as the README's daily trading example describes.
A small, known set of clients where you want to map connection groups to threads yourself, and a dependency-free header-only codebase (nine headers, about 56 KB) that you can vendor and audit.
when_not_to_use: You need durability through power loss or host reboot. The README says it does not persist data to disk: queues live in the page cache (mmap-ed files with no fsync) or in /dev/shm.
You need pub/sub, fan-out, topics, brokered storage or clients in other languages. It is C++-only and point-to-point.

The host is CPU-constrained or shared, or you need many connections. Every polling thread spins (the bundled echo example spins 2 threads in the SHM client and 3 in the server), and the README says performance degrades past about 1000 live connections.

Non-x86 or weakly ordered CPUs such as ARM. The shared-memory queue orders memory with compiler-only asm barriers and no hardware fences or atomics, which relies on x86 total store order. Issue #4 about ARM was only fixed in the test timer code. It is also Linux-only and IPv4-only.

Untrusted networks or multi-user hosts. There is no TLS, and authentication is only a user-defined login blob. The code assumes a logged-in client 'will not attack us' when it processes acks, and shared-memory files are created with mode 0666 (before umask).

integration.dependencies: none beyond Linux POSIX APIs (sockets, shm_open, mmap). The test build links -lrt -lpthread.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (test/build.sh uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3). It uses GCC builtins (__builtin_bswap*, __BYTE_ORDER__) and GNU inline asm, so it needs GCC or Clang. Tested compiler versions are not documented.
integration.platforms: Linux only; x86-64 is the only tested architecture (the benchmark host is a Xeon E5-2687W); IPv4 only
integration.thread_safety: Each connection is single-threaded: read and write it only from its polling thread (README Limitations), and push messages from other threads through your own queue. The server's PollCtl, PollTcp and PollShm can each run on its own thread, and the client's PollTcp and PollShm can run on separate threads. Cross-thread visibility uses compiler barriers, with no mutexes or atomics.

gotchas: The interface doc and examples show the constructor as (ptcp_dir, name), but TcpShmClient and TcpShmServer actually take (name, ptcp_dir) (open issue #6). The examples pass the same string for both, which hides the mismatch.

All capacities are compile-time Conf constants with small defaults: ShmQueueSize is 2048 B (32 64-byte blocks) and TcpQueueSize is 2000 B, and Alloc() returns nullptr when the queue is full, so the caller has to retry. In SHM mode every message takes whole 64-byte blocks, so a 12-byte message uses 64 B.

A server connection slot is bound to a client name at first login and stays bound until Stop(). Once MaxShmConnsPerGrp or MaxTcpConnsPerGrp distinct names have logged into a group, new names are rejected with 'Max client cnt exceeded'. If persisted sequence numbers disagree at login, the connection fails through OnSeqNumberMismatch and must be fixed by hand.

There are no transactions. A crash between Pop() and Push() can drop a response, and doing Push() before Pop() can duplicate one on recovery. The TCP side closes the connection if a message is larger than TcpRecvBufMaxSize, or if a send splits an 8-byte block and then gets EAGAIN; the connection recovers when it reconnects.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Every sibling is a broker or pub/sub system (Wisp/NATS, Zenoh, FluxMQ, Redpanda and Woodpecker as Kafka-class systems, SocketPro), so pick TCPSHM only for one C++ point-to-point link that needs sub-microsecond same-host latency and automatic resend after a crash, with no topics, fan-out or disk durability. Zenoh is the closer, maintained alternative if you need pub/sub with optional shared memory (a feature flag you must enable).
verified_claims_summary: The author ran an echo ping-pong on one Ubuntu 14.04 host (Xeon E5-2687W, 3.1 GHz, threads pinned), measuring average RTT only (total elapsed time divided by message count, no percentiles): 8.82 us over TCP loopback against 42.27 us for ZeroMQ REQ/REP over TCP (about 4.8x), and 0.338 us in SHM mode against 30.65 us for ZeroMQ IPC over a Unix domain socket (about 90x, but that compares busy-polled shared memory with a kernel socket). TCPSHM was built with g++ -std=c++11 -O3 (version not stated) while the ZeroMQ version, build and benchmark code are not published, and the README's 16/36/68/200-byte message mix matches the 2018 test code, but a 2020-05-04 commit changed HEAD's test to 4-16-byte payloads and a different clock, so HEAD does not reproduce the published numbers.
status_note: Abandoned: the last commit (2020-05-04) was a cache-padding tweak, and the open issues #5 (2020) and #6 (2025) have no replies. It is MIT-licensed, about 56 KB of dependency-free headers, and easy to vendor and patch.
